cards.text: Acts 4:25 says David spoke the words of this psalm. He opens with a big question about the whole world: 'Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?' Raging AND plotting, friend? That's a FULL schedule.

cards.question: True or false: When David says the peoples plot in vain, he means their plan is going to work.

cards.text: Then the kings of the earth take their stand, and the rulers gather together. Biggest meeting in the world, and NOBODY brought cookies.

cards.question: The kings of the earth and the rulers take their stand together. Who are they standing against?

answers.text: The LORD and His Anointed One
Moses and the elders of Israel
Elijah and the prophets of God

cards.text: Here's their big plan: 'Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords.' It's a group chat full of coworkers planning to tell off the boss, and EVERYBODY is typing in all caps.

cards.question: The kings want to break the chains and cast away the cords of the LORD and His Anointed One. What are they really saying?

answers.text: We won't be ruled by Them
We want Them to lead us
We need Them to protect us

cards.question: The kings are plotting down on earth. Meanwhile, the One enthroned in heaven ___.

cards.text: He laughs, and the Lord taunts them. Their plan is about as believable as me telling the whole bakery I'm only eating ONE cookie today.

cards.question: True or false: After laughing at the plotting kings, God just lets their plot slide.

cards.text: Then He rebukes them in His anger, and terrifies them in His fury. And what He says next shuts that whole meeting down.

cards.question: The kings are plotting against the LORD and His Anointed One. What does God announce He has already done?

answers.text: Sent a flood over the earth

cards.text: 'I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain.' The kings are still planning the takeover, and the King is already in place.
Now the King Himself speaks up. He says He will proclaim the decree the LORD spoke to Him.

cards.question: In the decree, the LORD tells the King, "You are My ___; today I have become Your Father."

cards.text: Friend, I know what it does to you when somebody calls you Papa. Then the LORD makes the Son an offer, and all He has to do is ask.

cards.question: True or false: The LORD offers to make the nations, even the ends of the earth, the Son's inheritance.
The LORD tells the Son what He will do to the raging nations. What picture does He use?

answers.text: Pottery shattered by an iron scepter
Chaff driven off by the wind
Grass withering in the summer sun

cards.text: Then the psalm turns straight to the rulers: 'Therefore be wise, O kings; be admonished, O judges of the earth.' And just like that, the group chat goes REAL quiet.

cards.question: The kings of the earth are told to be wise. What does being wise look like for them?

cards.text: Then comes an instruction for those kings: 'Kiss the Son.' Kings aren't used to taking orders, friend, but this is one to take.

cards.question: The kings are told to kiss the Son, or He may be angry and they could perish in their ___.
After all that warning to the kings, the psalm ends with good news. Who does it call blessed?

answers.text: All who take refuge in Him
All who rule over the earth

cards.text: Psalm 1 opened with 'Blessed is the man' (Psalm 1:1), and Psalm 2 closes on blessing too. The kings tried to break free, but the safest place in this whole psalm is taking refuge in Him.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 2 quotes "You are My ___; today I have become Your Father.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: 'The kings are still planning the takeover' stretches the text. In Psalm 2:3 the kings plan to break the chains and cast away the cords. That is throwing off rule, not taking over. This is a fact line, not a joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: 'Friend, I know what it does to you when somebody calls you Papa' doesn't make sense. The baker isn't the one called Papa, Papa Dorin is. The link to 'today I have become Your Father' is also left for the baker to work out, so a stranger would say 'huh?'.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The statement calls the ends of the earth the Son's 'inheritance'. Psalm 2:8 calls the nations His inheritance and the ends of the earth His possession. On a true or false card, this blurs what the text calls each thing.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The question says the LORD tells the Son what 'He will do to the raging nations'. In Psalm 2:9 it is the Son ('You will break them'), not the LORD. The 'them' there points back to the nations given as an inheritance in 2:8. Calling them the raging nations of 2:1 makes a connection the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The right answer 'Pottery shattered by an iron scepter' blends two separate lines. Psalm 2:9 says 'break them with an iron scepter' and 'shatter them like pottery'. It never says the scepter shatters pottery.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: 'Serving the LORD with fear' sounds like Scripture. 'Building a stronger army' and 'Signing a treaty with Egypt' sound like plain modern summaries. Right after a warning to be wise, the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: No card in stop 2 tells 'rejoice with trembling' from Psalm 2:11. It is the second half of what the kings are told to do, and the baker never sees it.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The last card mostly repeats the blessing just answered on card 10 and recaps the kings trying to break free. Only the Psalm 1:1 link is new, so it works as a recap card.

Stop 2 has almost no real humor. Cards 1 and 11 are plain telling. Card 8 ('Kings aren't used to taking orders, friend, but this is one to take') reads like a nice dad being pleasant. The only other attempts are the confusing Papa line on card 3 and the group chat callback on card 6.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: Card 1 says 'the King Himself speaks up' in Psalm 2:7. The verse doesn't name its speaker. It is someone the LORD calls 'My Son'. Saying this is the King installed in 2:6 links the two.
findings.question: Two rules point different ways here. One allows filling in 'what the text clearly implies'. The other says to leave open 'who is being spoken to' and 'how two things connect'. Does identifying the speaker of Psalm 2:7 as the King of 2:6 count as clearly implied, or should the card stay open (for example, 'Then a new voice speaks: someone the LORD calls His Son')?
